content: Hand, foot, and mouth disease is a highly contagious illness caused by various viruses. It predominantly affects infants and children under the age of five, although adults can occasionally contract the disease as well. The symptoms of hand, foot, and mouth disease include fever, painful blister-like sores inside the mouth, and a rash that may present as blisters on the hands, feet, or other parts of the body. While the disease is generally mild, most individuals recover within 7 to 10 days without complications. The disease spreads through close personal contact, such as kissing or hugging, as well as through respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing. It can also be transmitted via contact with feces (e.g., during diaper changes) or by touching contaminated objects or surfaces and then touching the eyes, nose, or mouth. Viruses responsible for hand, foot, and mouth disease are found worldwide. In temperate climates, the disease is more common during the summer and fall. Large and severe outbreaks, sometimes affecting thousands of individuals, frequently occur in certain countries in Asia. Currently, there is no vaccine available to prevent hand, foot, and mouth disease. However, there are several measures you can take to reduce your risk of infection: 1. Wash your hands frequently: Use soap and water, especially after using the bathroom and before eating. If soap and water are unavailable, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer. 2. Avoid touching your face: Do not touch your eyes, nose, or mouth with unclean hands. If you must touch your face, ensure your hands are clean. 3. Practice respiratory hygiene: Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your sleeve (not your hands) when coughing or sneezing. 4. Limit close contact with sick individuals: Avoid activities such as kissing, hugging, or sharing eating utensils and cups with people who are ill. To further prevent the spread of the disease, disinfect contaminated surfaces and items. If possible, first clean the items with soap and water, then disinfect them using a solution of chlorine bleach (prepared by mixing one tablespoon of bleach with four cups of water) or a cleaning product containing bleach. If you develop mouth sores and suspect you have hand, foot, and mouth disease, consider the following steps for symptom management: 1. Take over-the-counter medications to alleviate pain and reduce fever. Note that children should not be given aspirin. 2. Use mouthwashes or sprays designed to numb mouth pain. 3. Stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.
